skills.hero.1: It looks costly, and it isn't. Most of it is skills and workflows, so I could do the same thing tomorrow for a new company in half the time.
skills.icp-grid-from-client-site.1: Four agents read a company's whole site and work out which customers it can actually prove it serves. For Addvery: 4 ICPs out of 12 case studies.
skills.lead-router.1: Every lead gets an ICP, a language and a tactic, with the reason written down. Rules settled 4 of my 12 fictional leads for free. The model isn't wired in yet.
skills.linkedin-wall-builder.1: Someone's public LinkedIn posts as one wall, word for word, images and all. Mine took 6.6 seconds and $0.19 for 94 posts.
skills.onepassword-batch.1: Every key a task needs comes through one 1Password approval. Nothing gets printed, and the whole scraping run went by with no key on screen.
skills.operator-attention-controls.1: All the questions wait in one place and I answer them one at a time. If I don't, the helper decides and says why. When I closed everything by accident, it was all back in 9 minutes.
skills.outbound-workflow-factory.1: One copy file per ICP goes in, every GetSales sequence comes out, message 1 already set to the one variable. My 36-sequence example took 7 minutes.
skills.publish-leak-scan.1: Before anything gets committed or published, it's scanned for API keys, banned terms, emails and phone numbers. The 19 clips got a frame checked every two seconds.
skills.research-desk.1: About four questions per list, then three wildcards who chase the biggest question nobody asked. That got me 27 reports, all indexed.
skills.spec-driven-agent-team.1: One short plan says why and what. Each piece of work gets its own brief, its own AI helper and a log of every call it made without me. About 15 helpers, 739 commits, one day.
skills.stakeholder-landing-pages.1: Instead of one pitch for everyone, every decision-maker gets a page of their own, in their company's look. There are six.
skills.taste-grading-booth.1: I rate moments blind, and I keep 30% back so the scoring gets tested on my taste. I rated 126 moments. Next I turn that into a scoring guide.
skills.transcript-to-article.1: I talk, it writes a near-final article that still sounds like me, and I do the last 10%. Three of my articles started this way.

home.what.2: Instead of a CV, I did the work
home.what.3:
I'm a GTM engineer in Prague. GTM means go-to-market: I build the AI workflows that touch your pipeline, from researching an account to the first message a lead gets.

**This site is my job application to Addvery.** Most of it was built on 2 November, live on camera, in about 12 hours, with me directing a team of Claude Code sessions. It's in Addvery's brand, not mine. That's on purpose.

Below you'll find your own pages, my one argument, and one piece of the work, step by step.
home.what.quote: "You're going to get proof of what I can do. You don't need a CV."
home.what.quote_source: Me, on camera, 11:17 on build day
home.six.2: A page for each of you
home.six.3:
I tried to work out who a hire like me would need a yes from, using only public information. I landed on six people, and each of you would judge a GTM engineer differently, so each of you gets your own page.

(Honestly, these are guesses.)
home.argument.2: Put AI in your pipeline first
home.argument.3:
Up top I asked how you'll pay for AI. My answer is revenue, so **the first place I'd put AI is your pipeline**: your people get more done, and more work comes in at the same time.

And you don't have to pick between personalization and volume anymore. Now you can do both.
home.argument.figure.caption: Before AI you picked a spot on the line. Now you don't have to.
home.argument.figure.alt: A line from personalization to volume: before AI, one dot in the middle or at the volume end; now both ends are filled, so you can do both
home.argument.link: Why your first AI project should be your pipeline
home.proof.2: One lead, from a LinkedIn search to its first message
home.proof.3:
With AI you can run up to 30 to 50 different drip sequences (messages that go out one after another), by ICP, language and tactic. ICP means ideal customer profile, the kind of company you sell to. Then a classification model, an AI that sorts and doesn't write, puts each lead in exactly one.

My example has 36: Addvery's four ICPs, in Czech, German and English, with three openings each. Signal opens on news at their company, problem on a known pain, and proof on one of your case stories that looks like them.

**It doesn't matter how many sequences you have. It matters who gets put into which one.**
home.proof.fiction: **Everything below is made up:** the lead, the company and the message. The 36 sequences sit switched off in GetSales, my outreach tool, and nothing sends.
home.proof.card.title: The lead, as a LinkedIn search exports it
home.proof.step1.title: 1. Rules go first
home.proof.step1.lead: They're free and exact, and anyone on your team can check them.
home.proof.step1.rule_industry: "Entertainment Providers" doesn't match any industry rule, so it can't tell yet.
home.proof.step1.rule_language: It's in Czechia with a Czech profile, so it gets Czech.
home.proof.step1.rule_news: There's no news from the last 90 days, so no signal opening.
home.proof.step2.title: 2. Then Jev, for what the rules can't settle
home.proof.step2.lead: Jev is TypeSafe's classification model. It picks from a short list and says how sure it is.
home.proof.step2.jev_icp: It reads "paid streaming service selling subscriptions online" and picks telco CVM: telco, pay-TV and streaming operators.
home.proof.step2.rule_staff: It has 600 staff, over the 500 minimum for telco.
home.proof.step2.jev_case: Does it look like one of your case stories? Yes, a streaming launch like Oneplay, so it gets the proof opening.
home.proof.step2.clip.caption: "This tool is one of the coolest tools that have come out in AI, and no one's heard of it, because it's not an LLM."
home.proof.step2.clip.label: What Jev is
home.proof.step3.title: 3. A person, when Jev isn't sure
home.proof.step3.text: An answer only counts if Jev is at least 75% sure and 25 points ahead of its second choice. Otherwise a person decides.
home.proof.step3.caveat: Honest caveat: in this run a person labelled both answers instead of Jev. That's how it starts for real anyway, right?
home.proof.step4.title: 4. Exactly one sequence
home.proof.step4.text: It lands in Telco CVM, Czech, proof, with its reason right next to it.
home.proof.matrix_hit_title: Litware Stream CZ (fictional): a Czech streaming service, sorted into Telco CVM (telco, pay-TV and streaming)
home.proof.step5.title: 5. Its first message
home.proof.step5.message_cs: Dobrý den, pro streamovací službu, jako je ta vaše, jsme vedli spuštění nové platformy včetně převodu stávajících předplatitelů a start proběhl v plánovaném termínu. Rádi vám ukážeme, co z toho by se hodilo pro Litware Stream.
home.proof.step5.message_en: Hello. For a streaming service like yours, we led the launch of a new platform, including moving the existing subscribers over, and it went live on the planned date. We'd be glad to show you which parts of that would fit Litware Stream.
home.proof.twelve: I ran twelve made-up leads through it. Rules alone placed 4, 7 needed Jev, and 1 fit nothing. That one just gets logged with its reason, and nobody writes to it.
home.team.2: Then I ran the same model on Addvery's own team
home.team.3:
On build day I started counting Addvery's people on LinkedIn by hand, and then I stopped: "Why am I doing this? This is such something an assistant can do."

So the same kind of model read the public profiles and posts of Addvery's 56 staff, with no login, and answered one question: who sends outreach?

**Nobody at Addvery has a sales, business development or revenue operations title. The model still rates 10 people as likely doing outreach.** That's a signal, not a fact, but it's the first thing I want to know about any account. Who actually sells?

It cost $0.003, and I only show counts, never names.
home.team.figure.caption: Addvery's 56 staff on LinkedIn, as counts. No names.
home.team.figure.alt: LinkedIn activity board: how many in each function posted in the last 90 days, what the 50 posts were about, and three counts: 0 sales titles, 10 people likely doing outreach, 4 who posted a call to action for clients.
home.build.2: One person, a team of Claude Code sessions
home.build.3:
Most of this site was built in one recorded day. I directed more than 15 Claude Code sessions, each with one job and its own rules, all working from one written plan.

Not everything went well. At 13:20 I tried to close one session I didn't need, and closed all of them instead.
home.build.clip.caption: "I ended all sessions, including all the ones that handle the recording."
home.build.clip.label: I closed every session
home.build.4:
A fresh session brought every one of them back in under ten minutes. (I was hoping for a 15-minute setback, not an hour and a half.)

At 13:44 I asked for the fix as a skill:
home.build.quote: "Please go ahead and codify that as a skill, so that if I need to use it again, it's an instant fix."
home.build.5: Most of the build is skills like that one. It took me 12 hours, but **once it's built, it's built**, and I could do the same thing tomorrow with a new company in half the time.

home.about.3:
I spent 10 years freelancing in B2B marketing and over 20 years teaching, eight of them teaching English to Czechs. Then I took an AI sabbatical: nine months of nothing but building in Claude Code, 40 to 50 hours a week.

I've lived in Prague for over a decade, and my Czech is B1 to B2. Now I want to apply what I've learned to a real company, and get the satisfaction of making numbers go up.

Earlier I said I could do this again for a new company. **To be clear, I don't want there to be a next company.**
home.proof.step5.note.1: **AI wrote this message, and I didn't approve it.** I write my real messages by hand, every one. (After 8 years, it's the one thing I still write better than Claude.)
home.proof.step5.note.2: **The first message is always custom**, whichever sequence the lead lands in. When everyone's blasting you with messages, the only thing that gets one read is being different. So it's built from:
home.proof.step5.inputs.3: months of tracking: news, new hires, job changes
home.proof.step5.note.close: All so it can say one thing: I'm not shotgun blasting here, you're my number one priority.
